results.content: The application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in archaeology, art and the humanities is revolutionizing how researchers interpret, visualize and reconstruct material culture, from the past to the present [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/8/3/102#B1-heritage-08-00102)]. The second analysis of the heatmaps ([Figure 10](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/8/3/102#fig_body_display_heritage-08-00102-f010)) provides a visualization of three metrics (SSIM, MSE, and similarity) comparing the original image and the AI-generated image. Saliency maps generated by AI models offer a unique perspective on how machines “see” art [[40](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/8/3/102#B40-heritage-08-00102)]. Comparing AI-generated saliency maps with human gaze patterns provides insights into both human and machine perception [[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/8/3/102#B41-heritage-08-00102)]. For example, an AI model might be programmed to generate abstract art that maximizes saliency in certain regions, creating compositions that naturally draw the viewer’s eye [[45](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/8/3/102#B45-heritage-08-00102)]. By leveraging cutting-edge technologies such as AI-generated simulations, eye-tracking experiments, and saliency map analyses, it was possible to explore how these approaches contribute to understanding human interaction with cultural heritage [[49](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/8/3/102#B49-heritage-08-00102)] and reconstructing multiple narratives of the past.
